title: Chabad's open doors
hook: Chabad centers worldwide welcome Jews of every background

segments.voice: Last week ended on tradition as home: Sephardi and Mizrahi synagogues open to a wide range of observance. Today, a Hasidic movement that made the open door its whole method.

A backpacker lands in a city on the far side of the world on a Friday afternoon. No plans, no friends, a phone at four percent. Someone at the hostel says: there's a Chabad house a few streets away, they do dinner. She goes, half expecting to be turned away for not knowing the prayers. Instead a young couple opens the door, pulls up another chair, and puts a bowl of soup in front of her. Nobody asks how observant she is. A child hands her a song sheet. Today is about that door.
screen: `FRIDAY, FAR FROM HOME.` → `A CHAIR PULLED UP.` → `NOBODY ASKS HOW OBSERVANT.`

segments.voice: Chabad's open doors. First, who they are. Chabad is a Hasidic movement, fully Orthodox, the line of Rabbi Shneur Zalman, whom you met among the Hasidic masters. The movement explains its name as three Hebrew words, chochmah, binah, da'at: wisdom, understanding, knowledge. Its teaching asks the mind to lead the heart. Second, the emissaries. Its leader, known simply as the Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, sent young couples out as shluchim, emissaries, to cities, campuses and far-off towns, to settle there and stay. A Chabad house is often their own home, with the dining table stretched long. Third, the welcome. A Chabad center doesn't ask a Jew to join, sign, or already keep the law before coming in. A Passover seder for anyone who shows up. Candles handed out on a Friday. A man on a busy sidewalk offered the chance to put on tefillin for a minute. The idea underneath: every single commandment, done once, by anyone, matters. Fourth, the oldest picture behind it. Genesis says Abraham "sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." When three strangers appeared, "he ran to meet them from the tent door." The rabbis told that Abraham's tent was open on all four sides, so a guest never had to look for the entrance. A Chabad house echoes that tent. Not every Jew shares Chabad's theology or style, and some argue with parts of it. Today is about the open door: a tent with its sides rolled up.
screen: `WISDOM, UNDERSTANDING, KNOWLEDGE.` · `EMISSARIES WHO STAY.` · `NO TEST AT THE DOOR.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, OPEN ON ALL SIDES.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: Picture a tent with all four sides rolled up. Then remember a time someone pulled up a chair for you, a meal you were invited to, a door that opened before you knocked: who was it, and what didn't they ask you? Stay a few breaths with what it was like to be let in, and if you pray, give thanks for that person.
Chabad's open doors. A Hasidic, Orthodox movement whose emissaries settle in towns and campuses and welcome Jews of every background, no test at the door. Today's word.
Your line: open doors. One extra chair can be a whole welcome. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Chabad emissaries, often married couples, run Chabad houses and centers that host Shabbat meals, holiday events and classes open to Jews of any background, and offer passersby the chance to do a single commandment, like putting on tefillin.
